segments.en: At sunset along the White Nile, herds of long-horned cattle walk home through tall grass, the dust glowing gold behind them. This is South Sudan, one of the world's youngest countries, independent since 2011.
For many communities, among them the Dinka and the Nuer, cattle are far more than animals. They are wealth, pride and friendship, and a young man may compose songs in praise of his favourite ox.
In the middle of the country lies the Sudd, one of Africa's largest wetlands, a vast maze of papyrus and quiet channels where the Nile spreads out and slows down.
Every year, great herds of antelope, like the white-eared kob and the tiang, travel across the grasslands in search of water and grazing, one of the great animal journeys of Africa.
More than sixty languages are spoken here. English is the official language, and in the markets many people chat in a local form of Arabic often called Juba Arabic.
The capital, Juba, sits on the banks of the White Nile. Boats and bicycles, busy markets and music from radios give the city its rhythm from morning until night.
A common meal is asida, a thick porridge of sorghum or maize, eaten with a stew of okra, greens or fish. Kisra, a thin sourdough flatbread, is another favourite, torn and dipped into sauces.
Greetings matter. People shake hands warmly, sometimes touching their right arm with the left hand as a sign of respect, and take time to ask after your family.
Traditional wrestling is hugely popular. Young men from different communities meet in the ring while crowds sing, drum and cheer, and matches have become a joyful way of bringing people together.
Basketball is another great passion, and the national team has thrilled fans by competing on the world stage.
In the far south, the Imatong Mountains rise green and cool, while in the east, the plains around Boma stretch wide beneath enormous skies.
Look out for beadwork, carved wooden stools and the patterns painted for celebrations, each carrying the style of a particular community and passed down through families.
People here are resilient, hopeful and generous with a smile. Follow the Nile upstream to the south, and Uganda is waiting for you.
